3.1.2.3-r1.burton_quote: the cause of this poverty was his honesty
3.1.2.3-r1.translation: [The cause of his poverty was] philosophy, as for most people it was honesty.

3.1.2.3-r10.burton_quote: O sweet bands (Seneca exclaims), which so happily combine, that those which are bound by them love their binders, desiring withal, much more harder to be bound, and as so many Geryons to be united into one

3.1.2.3-r12.burton_quote: with like endeavour, affection, and piety, I have undertaken to write his life; since my fortunes will not give me leave to make a more sumptuous monument, I will perform those rites to his sacred ashes, which a small perhaps, but a liberal wit can afford

3.1.2.3-r2.burton_quote: and they bade him wash himself, and as he was worthy, take upon him the style and spirit of a King, continue his continency and the rest of his good parts

3.1.2.3-r3.burton_quote: you that scorn all but riches, and give no esteem to virtue, except they be wealthy withal, Q. Cincinnatus had but four acres, and by the consent of the Senate was chosen Dictator of Rome

3.1.2.3-r6.burton_quote: There is a peculiar beauty of justice, an inward beauty, which we see with the eyes of our hearts, love, and are enamoured with, as in Martyrs, though their bodies be torn in pieces with wild beasts
3.1.2.3-r6.translation: even if they were otherwise ugly

3.1.2.3-r7.burton_quote: wisdom and valour according to Xenophon, especially deserve the name of beauty

3.1.2.3-r8.burton_quote: there was a divine Majesty in his looks, it shined like Lightning, and drew all men to it
